abstract: Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence, and Recovery (TPPR) data are essential for forensic activity level evaluations (ALE); however, concerns remain regarding the accessibility of relevant literature. This study investigated whether automated literature retrieval and natural language processing (NLP) methods could be used to identify and characterize TPPR studies. Existing forensic repositories were combined with records retrieved through the Web of Science Application Programming Interface (API) and enriched with bibliographic metadata, producing a corpus of 3,279 unique records. Automated retrieval tools were evaluated, and transformer-based topic modeling was applied to examine the breadth of the literature. The results showed that database APIs provided the most reliable mechanism for literature retrieval, while topic modeling identified meaningful groupings corresponding to major forensic disciplines and trace evidence types. The findings indicate that TPPR literature exists and that automated methods can support its discovery and organization. Although the availability of literature does not necessarily imply suitability for ALE, the results suggest that the principal challenge is the discovery, assessment, and reuse of published studies rather than their absence. Automated retrieval, semantic search, and quality assessment frameworks may improve access to relevant evidence and support the development of forensic knowledge systems for evaluative reporting and Bayesian network construction.
